The Interview Bar

What live UI rounds are actually scoring

The Junior Approach

Creates a single monolithic component with 15 boolean flags (isOpen, hasHeader, showArrow, isSearchable). Mouse-only clicks. Zero keyboard support. Fails screen reader accessibility.

The Senior Approach

Designs an expressive, composable API using Compound Components. Separates state with custom hooks. Manages focus traps, roving tabindex, and WAI-ARIA roles out of the box.

Senior engineers don't just make pixels appear on screen — they author component APIs that other developers love using and that all users can navigate.

The Landscape

Six React patterns from javascriptpatterns.dev

1 · Con / Pres

Separating business logic & data fetching from pure UI rendering markup.

2 · HOC

Higher-Order Components. Enhancing components with cross-cutting abilities.

3 · Render Props

Inverting control by passing a function that returns JSX based on internal state.

4 · Hooks

Extracting reusable stateful behavior into pure functions without tree nesting.

5 · Provider

Passing state globally through the Fiber tree without prop drilling.

6 · Compound

Cohesive sub-components (<Select.Option>) sharing implicit state.

Part 1 · Component API Design

The five prop categories

Every prop on a component must belong to one of five distinct roles:
CategoryRoleExamples
1 · Data PropsWhat the component displaysusers={data}, totalCount={42}
2 · Event PropsHow parent reacts to actionsonSelect={(id) => ...}, onClose={fn}
3 · Config PropsBehavioral switches & modemode="single", size="lg"
4 · Style PropsCosmetic adjustmentsclassName, variant="ghost"
5 · Slot PropsInverted layout blocksheader={...}, children
The Anti-Pattern: Boolean prop proliferation. Adding isUserModal, isAdminModal, isCheckoutModal creates an unmaintainable combinatorial explosion.

API Design · State Contract

Controlled vs Uncontrolled: The single source of truth

Controlled: Parent Owns State

function Parent() {
  const [val, setVal] = useState('');
  return <Input value={val} onChange={setVal} />;
}

Parent dictates value. Essential for instant validation, conditional formatting, and synchronizing multiple inputs.

Uncontrolled: DOM Owns State

function Parent() {
  const inputRef = useRef();
  return <Input defaultValue='init' ref={inputRef} />;
}

State lives in DOM. Read on-demand on form submit. Zero re-renders during keystrokes.

Senior Component Contract: Support controlled mode when value !== undefined, but fall back to internal uncontrolled state with defaultValue when omitted!

Part 2 · Container / Presentational

Separating state from rendering markup

Container Component (How things work)
function JobListContainer() {
  const { jobs, loading, error } = useJobs();
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('');

  if (loading) return <Spinner />;
  if (error) return <ErrorMessage />;

  return (
    <JobListView
      jobs={jobs}
      filter={filter}
      onFilterChange={setFilter}
    />
  );
}
Presentational Component (How things look)
function JobListView({ jobs, filter, onFilterChange }) {
  return (
    <section className="job-feed">
      <FilterBar value={filter} onChange={onFilterChange} />
      <ul>
        {jobs.map(j => <JobCard key={j.id} {...j} />)}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}

Container / Presentational · Evolution

How Custom Hooks replaced container components

You no longer need an extra JSX layer just to hold state.

The 2016 Paradigm (Component Wrapper)

Every data-fetching feature had two files: UserListContainer.jsx and UserListView.jsx. Resulted in deeply nested component trees in React DevTools.

The Modern Paradigm (Hook as Container)

Extract all fetching, sorting, and state into useUserList(). The UI component calls the hook directly at the top. The separation of concerns remains 100% intact!

Where Container Components Returned: Next.js Server Components! An RSC acts as the asynchronous server container, passing data to a 'use client' interactive presentational component.

Part 3 · HOC Pattern

Enhancing components with cross-cutting concerns

A Higher-Order Component is a pure function taking a component and returning an enhanced component.
function withAuth(WrappedComponent) {
  return function WithAuthComponent(props) {
    const { isAuthenticated, loading } = useAuth();

    if (loading) return <PageSkeleton />;
    if (!isAuthenticated) return <Redirect to="/login" />;

    return <WrappedComponent {...props} />;
  };
}

// Usage:
const ProtectedDashboard = withAuth(Dashboard);
Used extensively in legacy React codebases, Redux (connect), and Relay for telemetry, authentication, and layout wrappers.

HOC Pattern · Implementation Invariants

The three rules of writing a production HOC

1 · Pass-Through Props

Always forward unrelated props: {...props}. Never swallow props that the wrapped component expects.

2 · Wrap Display Name

Set WithAuth.displayName = `WithAuth(${Component.displayName})` so React DevTools error stacks remain readable.

3 · Forward Refs!

Wrap the HOC in React.forwardRef. If you don't, passing ref attaches to the wrapper instead of the underlying DOM element!

// Ref-forwarding HOC template
const withBorder = (Comp) => {
  return React.forwardRef((props, ref) => (
    <div className="border-wrapper">
      <Comp ref={ref} {...props} />
    </div>
  ));
};

HOC Pattern · Trade-offs

Why the React ecosystem moved away from HOCs

1 · Wrapper Hell

Inspecting DevTools showed 15 nested components: <WithRouter><WithTheme><WithAuth><WithRedux>.... Made debugging props and layouts a nightmare.

2 · Prop Name Collisions

If withUser and withProfile both inject a prop called data, the last HOC silently overwrites the first one without a compile error.

3 · Static Method Hoisting

Any static methods attached to the wrapped component are lost unless manually copied over using hoist-non-react-statics.

Hooks solved every single one of these three flaws without adding a single DOM node or wrapper component.

Part 4 · Render Props Pattern

Inverting control over rendering

A component shares its internal state by delegating rendering to a function prop.
// Toggle Component with Render Prop
function Toggle({ children }) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  const toggle = () => setOn(s => !s);

  // Invoke child as a render function
  return children({ on, toggle });
}

// Consumer decides the markup:
<Toggle>
  {({ on, toggle }) => (
    <button onClick={toggle}>
      Status: {on ? 'ACTIVE' : 'PAUSED'}
    </button>
  )}
</Toggle>

Inversion of Control

Toggle handles state transitions and boolean toggling.

The consumer has 100% control over what renders: button, switch, checkbox, or keyboard badge.

Unlike HOCs, there are zero prop collisions because arguments are scoped inside the callback function.

Render Props · Production Reality

Where Render Props still dominates today

Even after hooks, Render Props remains the gold standard for geometric & virtualization engines:

Virtual Lists & Windowing

<VirtualList items={jobs} itemHeight={60}>
  {({ item, index, style }) => (
    <div style={style}>
      <JobRow job={item} />
    </div>
  )}
</VirtualList>

Parent calculates top/height offsets; consumer formats the row.

Intersection & Visibility

<InView threshold={0.5}>
  {({ inView, ref }) => (
    <div ref={ref}>
      {inView ? <HeavyChart /> : <Skeleton />}
    </div>
  )}
</InView>

Attaches DOM observers and renders conditionally.

Render Props · Trade-offs

Callback pyramids vs dynamic flexibility

The Callback Pyramid (Callback Hell)

Composing multiple render prop components creates deep indentation:

<User>{u => (
  <Theme>{t => (
    <WindowSize>{w => (
      <App user={u} theme={t} size={w} />
    )}</WindowSize>
  )}</Theme>
)}</User>

The Hooks Contrast

Hooks flatten the exact same state extraction into linear top-level statements:

const u = useUser();
const t = useTheme();
const w = useWindowSize();
return <App user={u} theme={t} size={w} />;
Use Render Props when the component needs to render dynamic JSX fragments inside its own DOM container. Use Hooks when sharing pure state and logic.

Part 5 · Hooks Pattern

Stateful logic without component hierarchy

Custom hooks extract state, subscriptions, and DOM measurements into composable primitives.
// Custom Hook: useDebounce
function useDebounce(value, delay = 300) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);

  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      setDebounced(value);
    }, delay);

    return () => clearTimeout(timer);
  }, [value, delay]);

  return debounced;
}

// In Component:
const debouncedQuery = useDebounce(searchQuery, 400);

Why Hooks Won

  • Zero DOM bloatNo wrappers, no extra divs, no synthetic hierarchy
  • Full TypeScript inferenceReturns typed values and tuples natively
  • Composable chainingA custom hook can call 5 other custom hooks

Hooks Pattern · Engine Reality

Why the Rules of Hooks exist

React does not identify hooks by name. It tracks them as a singly linked list on the Fiber node.
If you call a hook inside an if (condition), Hook 2 is skipped on some renders. The list pointer shifts, and React returns Hook 3's state to Hook 2! Memory pointers get corrupt.

Hooks Pattern · Design System

Tuple vs Object: Designing custom hook return contracts

Tuple Return: [state, actions]

function useToggle(initial = false) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(initial);
  const toggle = useCallback(() => setOn(s => !s), []);
  return [on, toggle] as const;
}

// Easy to rename on call site:
const [isModalOpen, toggleModal] = useToggle();
const [isDrawerOpen, toggleDrawer] = useToggle();

Best for 1–2 values where renaming is common (like useState).

Object Return: { data, loading, ... }

function useQuery(key) {
  // ...
  return { data, error, isLoading, refetch };
}

// Consumers pick what they care about:
const { data, isLoading } = useQuery('users');

Best for 3+ values. Allows backwards-compatible additions without breaking positional arguments.

Part 6 · Provider Pattern

Passing state globally without prop drilling

React Context passes data directly down the Fiber tree to any descendant subscriber.
const ThemeContext = React.createContext(null);

export function ThemeProvider({ children }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('dark');

  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
      {children}
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useTheme() {
  const ctx = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useTheme must be used within ThemeProvider');
  return ctx;
}
Always export a custom hook (useTheme) with an invariant guard! It prevents silent null crashes when consumers forget the provider.

Provider Pattern · The Trap

The reference equality trap that re-renders everything

The Bug: Inline Object Value

<CountContext.Provider
  value={{ count, dispatch }}>
  {children}
</CountContext.Provider>

Every time CountProvider renders, a new object reference { count, dispatch } is created. Every component using useContext re-renders, even if count didn't change!

The Fix: Split State & Dispatch

<StateContext.Provider value={state}>
  <DispatchContext.Provider value={dispatch}>
    {children}
  </DispatchContext.Provider>
</StateContext.Provider>

Because dispatch identity never changes, buttons that only fire actions NEVER re-render when state changes!

Part 7 · Compound Pattern

Components that work together as one cohesive unit

From javascriptpatterns.dev: Sub-components sharing implicit state without prop drilling.
// Clean, declarative Consumer JSX
<Select defaultValue="eg" onChange={handleCountryChange}>
  <Select.Trigger placeholder="Select country" />
  <Select.List>
    <Select.Option value="eg">Egypt</Select.Option>
    <Select.Option value="sa">Saudi Arabia</Select.Option>
    <Select.Option value="ae">United Arab Emirates</Select.Option>
  </Select.List>
</Select>
Compare this to a monolithic <Select options={[...]} />. The Compound Pattern gives consumers complete control over DOM structure, styling, icon placement, and accessibility slots!

Compound Pattern · Implementation

Two approaches: React Context vs cloneElement

Approach A: React.cloneElement

Parent iterates over React.Children.map and clones children with extra injected props.

Fatal Flaw: Only works on immediate direct children! If the consumer wraps an <Option /> in a <div class="wrapper">, the cloned props are lost.

Approach B: React Context (Modern Standard)

Parent wraps children in an internal CompoundContext.Provider. Sub-components read state via useContext().

Winner: Works at arbitrary depth! Consumer can insert layout divs, grid wrappers, or animations anywhere between components.

21 / 28
Compound Pattern · Implementation Code

Building Compound Tabs in 25 lines

const TabsContext = React.createContext(null);

export function Tabs({ defaultValue, children }) {
  const [activeTab, setActiveTab] = useState(defaultValue);
  return (
    <TabsContext.Provider value={{ activeTab, setActiveTab }}>
      <div className="tabs-root">{children}</div>
    </TabsContext.Provider>
  );
}

Tabs.Tab = function Tab({ value, children }) {
  const { activeTab, setActiveTab } = useContext(TabsContext);
  const isSelected = activeTab === value;
  return (
    <button
      role="tab"
      aria-selected={isSelected}
      className={isSelected ? 'tab-active' : 'tab'}
      onClick={() => setActiveTab(value)}>
      {children}
    </button>
  );
};

Tabs.Panel = function Panel({ value, children }) {
  const { activeTab } = useContext(TabsContext);
  if (activeTab !== value) return null;
  return <div role="tabpanel">{children}</div>;
};

Accessibility · WAI-ARIA

The screen reader contract

A component is not finished when the CSS is styled; it is finished when ARIA attributes speak the truth.
RoleRequired ARIA AttributesTarget Element
comboboxaria-expanded, aria-autocomplete, aria-controlsSearch input
listboxaria-label, tabIndex="-1"Popup dropdown list
optionaria-selected="true|false", id="opt-N"List items
dialogaria-modal="true", aria-labelledby="title-id"Modal overlay
statusaria-live="polite"Toast / notification
When an autocomplete option is highlighted with Arrow keys, the input MUST update aria-activedescendant="opt-id" so screen readers announce the item without stealing keyboard focus!

Accessibility · Keyboard Navigation

Focus traps & roving tabindex

Roving tabindex (Lists & Menus)

A menu should only have one Tab stop. Pressing Tab lands on the active item.

Navigating options uses ↑ and ↓ arrows by toggling tabIndex={isActive ? 0 : -1} and calling el.focus().

Focus Trap (Modal Dialogs)

When a modal opens, focus must be trapped inside. Pressing Tab on the last element cycles to the first element.

Pressing Escape closes the modal and restores focus to the trigger button that opened it!

Restoring focus on modal close is the single most common accessibility test question in senior frontend interviews.

Observer APIs · High-Performance Reactivity

The 3 Web Observers in UI engineering: 60fps without event bubbling

IntersectionObserver

50× faster than scroll listeners

Tracks sentinel visibility asynchronously. Eliminates 15ms setInterval coordinate polling.

Sentinel Pattern: Fires when bottom sentinel intersects; fetches next page and appends in 1 batch.

MutationObserver

Native subtree tracking

Tracks DOM changes without JS proxy wrappers. Essential for contenteditable editors & sandboxes.

Notion Pattern: Never observe 10,000 nodes! Observe only the active line; guard against recursive self-firing.

ResizeObserver

10× faster than window.onresize

Element-level dimensions without event bubbling. Uses logical inlineSize and blockSize for RTL/vertical text.

Trading Dashboards: Resizing 1 chart in a multi-grid updates only that chart's toolbar.

Virtualization · Architecture & Pooling

Why lazy scrolling fails & the fixed memory pool

The Flaw of Lazy Scrolling

Appending 5,000 DOM nodes creates heavy C++ objects, takes >100ms per layout pass, and freezes UI during garbage collection.

Virtualization Rule: Keep 100,000 items in virtual JS memory. Render only 20 nodes in the DOM forever.

The Half-Swapping Algorithm

// Fixed limit = 2 * pageSize (e.g. 20 nodes total)
if (this.pool.length >= this.limit) {
  // Slice the top 10 elements scrolled out of view
  const recycle = this.pool.slice(0, this.pageSize);
  const unchanged = this.pool.slice(this.pageSize);

  // Swap halves in memory array:
  this.pool = [...unchanged, ...recycle];
}

Pure Memory Operation: Slicing and swapping happens in JS array pointers first — zero DOM thrashing!

Virtualization · Mutation & Compositing

In-place template updates & zero-reflow GPU positioning

In-Place Data Mutation

function updateTemplate(element, datum) {
  // Mutates existing live DOM node references
  element.querySelector('.title').textContent = datum.title;
  element.querySelector('.body').textContent = datum.body;
  return element;
}

Recycled nodes receive new data while scrolled out of view. No nodes are created or destroyed, eliminating GC pauses!

Zero-Reflow GPU Math

// Sequential Y coordinate calculation:
for (let i = 0; i < this.pool.length; i++) {
  const prev = this.pool.at(i - 1);
  const prevY = y(prev);
  const newY = (prevY === null)
    ? 0
    : prevY + prev.getBoundingClientRect().height + (2 * MARGIN);

  // GPU Composite only: ZERO Layout Pass!
  this.pool[i].style.transform = `translateY(${newY}px)`;
}

Each card uses position: absolute. Moving via translateY skips layout and paint entirely.

Virtualization · Complete Architecture

The VirtualList state machine: production vanilla JS

class VirtualList {
  async handleBottomObserver() {
    const data = await this.getPage(this.end);
    if (this.pool.length < this.limit) {
      // Warmup Phase: Append initial nodes using DocumentFragment
      const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
      data.forEach(d => {
        const card = this.getTemplate(d);
        this.pool.push(card);
        frag.appendChild(card);
      });
      this.list.appendChild(frag);
    } else {
      // Recycling Phase: Slice, Swap Halves, Update In-Place
      const recycle = this.pool.slice(0, this.pageSize);
      const unchanged = this.pool.slice(this.pageSize);
      this.pool = [...unchanged, ...recycle];
      this.updateData(recycle, data); // In-place textContent update
    }
    this.updateElementPosition();    // translateY math for all cards
    this.updateObservers();          // Relocate top & bottom sentinels via translateY
    this.end++;
  }
}
This single 35-line state machine renders 100,000 items with constant 60fps, fixed memory usage, and bidirectional scrolling.

Module 07 · The Complete Answer

The UI engineering playbook: live coding framework & recap

The 4-Step Live Coding Framework

  • 1 · Contract (5 min): Controlled vs uncontrolled? ARIA role? Keyboard loop? Virtualization budget?
  • 2 · Scaffold (10 min): Write consumer JSX first (<List><Item>). Agree on API.
  • 3 · Wire State & Observers (15 min): Context provider or fixed pool; attach native observers.
  • 4 · Polish (10 min): Roving tabindex, focus restoration, and GPU-only translateY transforms.
